doc.title: Al Tinney interviewed by Monk Rowe, Buffalo, New York, October 14, 2002

title: Segregated audiences on a tour as band director
summary: Audiences were integrated in the theater but roped off on a southern circus-style tour where he was band director.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Did you get, in the theater when you were working, did they have an integrated audiences?

Yes, yes in the theater. But I went on a — what would you call these things now that people go on — almost like a circus. And I went on this one, this circus bit like. And I was the band director for it. And they were separated audiences because we went to the seaboard, all the way down south. And there was audiences, half this side, there was a rope down the middle.
Oh the old, the rope thing.
Yeah. And what the hell, it wasn’t bad, I mean everybody knew what was happening.
What they were supposed to do. What year would that have been? Or around what time?
’39 I think it was. “38, ’39. Something around there.
And did you have an integrated band?

No, no I didn’t have an integrated band. I had comedians and whatnot. And one comedian, he used to knock me out, he would have this black face stuff on you know, and he would get in front of the audience and says, “Yep it was me and these six other white boys standing on the corner.” And I used to crack up every time he said that. I don’t know why. But it was funny to me you know. It was funny to me.
